messages.author: e498b38f01df2491
messages.subject: convergence - HDS
parts:
Dear all,

I am estimating density and abundance of whales using hierarchical line-transect sampling model.
To validate the model, I am performing a small simulated study. 

When I check the jags output of the model for the simulated dataset, the true parameter values are covered by the 95% probability interval and Rhat is very close to 1. Traceplots for all parameters also show good indication of stationarity.

Nevertheless, when I perform some tests from coda package the indications are showing the opposite. For example, the Geweke statistics are not between -2 and 2 and in the Raftery diagnostics the dependence factor are larger than 5.

Have someone passed to a similar issue? Can I argue that chains converged based on traceplots, Rhat and 95%P.I. covering the true parameter values?

Thank you in advance for you help.

Best regards,
Heloise.

messages.author: 39971e2c19b8ec70
messages.subject: Re: convergence - HDS
parts:
Hi Heloise,

I have never checked for Geweke or Raftery... just looking at PSRF and
MPSRF... reported by gelman.diag(). Which can be tricky though, because
sometimes you might get PSRF close to 1 and chains not converging and vice
versa, see:

http://stats.stackexchange.com/a/139374/5509

thats why Marc recommends to always visually check the traceplots... Which
might be tricky if you have plenty of models, but I just made scripts to
generate all the plots automatically and I just quickly skim over them..

Tomas

PS: I am not sure if there is any difference between R-hat and PSRF, see
this discussion: http://stats.stackexchange.com/q/125306/5509

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: convergence - HDS
parts:
The PSRF is the same as r-hat (with MPSRF equivalent to the multivariate r-hat), so I'm not sure that this will provide different information. I think of the Raftery as being useful for figuring out how long to run a single chain in order to achieve a certain level of accuracy, but I'm not sure there's any formal way to convert the dependence value for a single chain into a requisite length for multiple chains (but curious to hear if there is!).  The Geweke is designed to find the non-stationarity displayed in Marc's post. My extremely speculative guess is that your chains are converging, but the burn-in could run a little longer.  If you chop out some of the initial saved iterations, does the Geweke change at all? 

John
